prompt: Governments should spend more money on railways than on roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
The question of how governments should allocate infrastructure spending is among the most consequential in contemporary urban policy. While roads retain clear value in rural connectivity, I would argue that the case for prioritising railway investment is compelling, particularly given the twin pressures of urbanisation and climate change.

The primary justification for redirecting funds towards railways is environmental. Rail transport generates, on average, approximately six times fewer carbon emissions per passenger kilometre than private car travel. In countries such as Japan and Switzerland, sustained investment in high-speed and commuter rail networks has demonstrably reduced urban air pollution and contributed to national carbon reduction targets. By contrast, the construction of new road capacity is well-documented to induce demand — a phenomenon known as induced traffic — meaning that new roads generate additional car journeys rather than alleviating congestion.

A further argument concerns economic efficiency and urban density. As cities expand, roads become an increasingly inefficient means of moving large numbers of people. A single underground line can transport up to 80,000 passengers per hour in each direction; no road can come close to matching this capacity. Governments that continue to prioritise road expenditure are, in effect, investing in infrastructure whose returns diminish as the populations it serves grow.

In conclusion, although roads remain essential for rural communities and freight logistics, the balance of evidence supports greater investment in railways for urban and inter-city transport. The environmental and capacity benefits of rail are not marginal improvements — they represent a structural shift in how modern societies can move sustainably.
